prompt: What does it mean to call an addition reaction regiospecific?

choices.text: Only one of the two possible orientations of addition occurs
Both possible orientations of addition occur in equal amounts
choices.why: That gives a mixture. Regiospecific means only one orientation occurs, giving a single product.

choices.text: Only one stereoisomer, cis or trans, is formed in the addition
choices.why: Regiospecific is about which carbon gets which part of the reagent, not about cis–trans geometry.

choices.text: The addition takes place in a single step, with no intermediate
choices.why: Electrophilic addition takes two steps. Regiospecific refers to the orientation of the addition.

explanation: When an unsymmetrically substituted alkene gives a single addition product rather than a mixture, the reaction is regiospecific: only one of two possible orientations of addition occurs. For example, 2-methylpropene and HCl give only 2-chloro-2-methylpropane.

prompt: What does Markovnikov's rule say about the addition of HX to an alkene?

choices.text: The H attaches to the carbon with fewer alkyl substituents, and the X to the carbon with more
The H attaches to the carbon with more alkyl substituents, and the X to the carbon with fewer
choices.why: That's the reverse. X ends up on the more substituted carbon.

choices.text: Both H and X attach to the carbon with more alkyl substituents
choices.why: H and X add to the two different carbons of the double bond.

choices.text: The X always attaches to the carbon at the end of the chain
choices.why: Position in the chain isn't the criterion; the number of alkyl substituents is. In 2-methylpropene, Cl goes to the inner carbon.

explanation: Markovnikov's rule (1869): in the addition of HX to an alkene, the H attaches to the carbon with fewer alkyl substituents and the X attaches to the carbon with more alkyl substituents.

choices.why: That product would need Cl on the CH2 carbon, which has no alkyl substituents. It isn't formed.
A mixture might be expected, but 2-chloro-2-methylpropane is the sole product.
Addition uses up the double bond, so the product has no double bond.

explanation: 2-Methylpropene might give both 2-chloro-2-methylpropane and 1-chloro-2-methylpropane, but it gives only 2-chloro-2-methylpropane. H adds to the CH2 carbon (no alkyl groups) and Cl to the carbon with two methyls.

prompt: How is Markovnikov's rule restated in terms of the reaction intermediate?

choices.text: The more highly substituted carbocation is formed as the intermediate rather than the less highly substituted one
The less highly substituted carbocation is formed as the intermediate rather than the more highly substituted one
choices.why: That's the reverse: the more substituted cation forms.

choices.text: The more highly substituted radical is formed as the intermediate rather than the less highly substituted one
choices.why: Electrophilic additions go through carbocations, not radicals.

choices.text: The more highly substituted alkene is formed as the intermediate rather than the less highly substituted one
choices.why: The intermediate is a carbocation, formed by adding H+ to the alkene.

explanation: Because carbocations are intermediates in these reactions, Markovnikov's rule can be restated: in the addition of HX to an alkene, the more highly substituted carbocation is formed as the intermediate rather than the less highly substituted one.

prompt: Which carbocation forms when H+ adds to 2-methylpropene, (CH3)2C=CH2?

choices.why: That cation would come from adding H+ to the inner carbon; the more substituted tertiary cation forms instead.
That cation has a different carbon skeleton, so it can't come from protonating 2-methylpropene.
Adding H+ to an alkene doesn't break the carbon chain. The tertiary cation forms.

explanation: Adding H+ to the CH2 carbon of 2-methylpropene gives the tertiary carbocation (CH3)3C+ rather than the alternative primary carbocation, (CH3)2CHCH2+. The halide ion then adds to the tertiary carbon.

choices.why: That would put Br on the double-bond carbon with fewer alkyl substituents. It isn't formed.
The double-bond carbons are differently substituted, so only one orientation occurs.
The methyl group stays in the product; only H and Br are added.

explanation: In 1-methylcyclohexene, C1 has two alkyl substituents (the methyl and a ring carbon) and C2 has one. H adds to C2 and Br to C1, through a tertiary rather than a secondary carbocation: 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane.

prompt: When 2-pentene, CH3CH=CHCH2CH3, reacts with HBr, how many different addition products form?
explanation: Each end of the double bond carries one alkyl substituent, so neither orientation is favored. A mixture forms: 2-bromopentane and 3-bromopentane.

prompt: What would you expect from the reaction of 2-hexene, CH3CH=CHCH2CH2CH3, with HBr?

choices.text: Only 2-bromohexane, since Br adds nearer the chain end
choices.why: Both double-bond carbons have one alkyl substituent, so Markovnikov's rule doesn't favor either one.

choices.text: Only 3-bromohexane, since Br adds to the carbon with the larger group
choices.why: Markovnikov's rule counts alkyl substituents, not their size, and each double-bond carbon has one.

choices.text: Only 1-bromohexane, since Br adds to the end carbon
choices.why: C1 isn't a double-bond carbon in 2-hexene, so simple addition can't put Br there.

explanation: C2 carries a methyl and C3 carries a propyl: one alkyl substituent each. When both double-bond carbons have the same degree of substitution, a mixture of addition products results, here 2-bromohexane and 3-bromohexane.

prompt: What product would you expect from the reaction of 1-ethylcyclopentene with HCl?

choices.why: That puts Cl on C2, which has only one alkyl group. Cl goes to C1, which has two.
That would be the product of adding H2. HCl adds H and Cl.
An alcohol forms when water adds. With HCl the product is an alkyl chloride.

explanation: Following Worked Example 7.8.1: H+ adds to the double-bond carbon with one alkyl group (C2 of the ring), and Cl adds to the carbon with two alkyl groups (C1). The product is 1-chloro-1-ethylcyclopentane.

prompt: According to Markovnikov's rule, how many different alkenes (not counting cis and trans isomers separately) could react with HCl to give 3-chloro-3-methylhexane, CH3CH2C(Cl)(CH3)CH2CH2CH3?
explanation: The carbon bearing Cl must have been a double-bond carbon. Its partner could be C2, C4, or the methyl carbon: 3-methyl-2-hexene, 3-methyl-3-hexene, or CH2=C(CH2CH3)CH2CH2CH3. In each, C3 is the more substituted double-bond carbon, so all three give 3-chloro-3-methylhexane (Worked Example 7.8.2).

prompt: What product forms when 2-methyl-2-pentene, (CH3)2C=CHCH2CH3, reacts with HBr?

choices.why: That puts Br on C3, which has only one alkyl substituent. Br goes to C2, which has two.
C1 isn't a double-bond carbon, so simple addition can't put Br there.
The two double-bond carbons are differently substituted (two alkyl groups versus one), so only one product forms.

explanation: C2 carries two methyl groups (two alkyl substituents) and C3 carries one ethyl. H adds to C3 and Br to C2, giving 2-bromo-2-methylpentane.

prompt: What alcohol forms when 4-methyl-1-pentene, (CH3)2CHCH2CH=CH2, adds water in the presence of sulfuric acid?

choices.why: That puts OH on C1, which has no alkyl substituents. OH goes to C2, the more substituted double-bond carbon.
That puts OH on the branch carbon, which isn't part of the double bond. The OH goes to C2 counting from the CH2= end.
Adding water gives an alcohol. An alkane would come from adding H2.

explanation: Water adds like HX: H goes to C1 (no alkyl substituents) and OH to C2 (one alkyl substituent). The product is 4-methyl-2-pentanol.

prompt: Methylenecyclohexane is a cyclohexane ring with a =CH2 group double-bonded to one ring carbon. What does it give with HBr?

choices.why: That puts Br on the CH2 carbon, which has no alkyl substituents. Br goes to the ring carbon, which has two.
The Br and the new methyl group end up on the same ring carbon, since both come from the same double bond.
No carbon is lost; the =CH2 carbon becomes a methyl group.

explanation: The ring carbon of the double bond carries two alkyl groups (two ring carbons), while the =CH2 carbon carries none. H adds to the CH2, which becomes a methyl group, and Br adds to the ring carbon: 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane.

prompt: Which alkene would give 3-bromohexane as its only product with HBr?

choices.why: Both double-bond carbons of 2-hexene carry one alkyl group, so it gives a mixture of 2-bromohexane and 3-bromohexane.
Markovnikov addition to 1-hexene puts Br on C2, giving 2-bromohexane.
That has a different carbon skeleton; with HBr it gives 2-bromo-2-methylpentane.

explanation: 3-Hexene, CH3CH2CH=CHCH2CH3, is symmetrical: adding Br to either double-bond carbon gives the same compound, 3-bromohexane.

prompt: Which alkene would give 1-ethyl-1-iodocyclohexane with HI?

choices.why: Ethylcyclohexane has no double bond, so it can't add HI.
That would give 1-iodo-1-methylcyclohexane; the product needs an ethyl group.
Cyclohexene has no ethyl group; with HI it would give iodocyclohexane.

explanation: The carbon bearing I in the product must have been the more substituted double-bond carbon. In 1-ethylcyclohexene, C1 carries the ethyl and a ring carbon (two alkyl groups) and C2 carries one, so I adds to C1. (Ethylidenecyclohexane would also work.)
